Orpah
OR-puh
proper noun
Hebrew Orpah, perhaps “neck” or “she who turns the back,” the Moabite wife of Chilion.

📖 Biblical Definition

Orpah was a woman of Moab, the wife of Chilion the son of Elimelech and Naomi (Ruth 1:4). When her husband and his brother had died, and Naomi resolved to return to Bethlehem, Orpah set out with her, weeping; but at Naomi’s urging that the young widows return to their mothers’ houses, Orpah lifted up her voice and wept, kissed her mother-in-law, and went back to her people and her gods (Ruth 1:14). “Behold,” Naomi said to Ruth, “thy sister in law is gone back unto her people, and unto her gods: return thou after thy sister in law” (Ruth 1:15). But Ruth clave unto Naomi and would not turn back. Orpah is remembered forever in contrast to Ruth: both began the journey, both wept, both were urged to return; but Orpah turned back to Moab and its idols, and is heard of no more, while Ruth pressed on to the God of Israel and became an ancestress of David and of Christ. Her name itself, linked to the neck or the turning of the back, fits her parting. Orpah stands as a solemn type of those who come near to the people of God and to the borders of faith, yet draw back, preferring the familiar gods of their own country to the living LORD.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Moabite wife of Chilion, who wept but turned back to her people and her gods, in contrast to Ruth.

expand to see more

ORPAH, a woman of Moab, the wife of Chilion (Ruth 1:4).

When widowed, she set out with Naomi toward Bethlehem.

At Naomi’s urging she kissed her and turned back (Ruth 1:14).

She returned to her people and her gods (Ruth 1:15).

She stands forever in contrast to Ruth, who clave to the LORD.

📖 Key Scripture

Ruth 1:4 — "And they took them wives of the women of Moab; the name of the one was Orpah, and the name of the other Ruth: and they dwelled there about ten years."

Ruth 1:14 — "And they lifted up their voice, and wept again: and Orpah kissed her mother in law; but Ruth clave unto her."

Ruth 1:15 — "And she said, Behold, thy sister in law is gone back unto her people, and unto her gods: return thou after thy sister in law."

Ruth 1:16 — "And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; she is a type of those who come near to faith yet draw back.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the warning of Orpah’s turning back. She wept, she kissed, she set out on the road; outwardly her affection seemed as great as Ruth’s. Yet when the cost was counted, she returned to her people and her gods, while Ruth pressed on. Many come near to the kingdom of God with tears and good beginnings, yet draw back to the world. The Scripture honours not the one who starts but the one who cleaves to the end.

Orpah and Ruth together teach that natural ties and warm feelings are not saving faith. Both were Moabitesses, both married into the same household, both wept at the parting; but one returned to Chemosh and one embraced the LORD. The dividing line was not blood or sentiment but the cleaving of the heart to the God of Israel. “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1Jn 2:19) is the abiding lesson of the woman who turned back.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name is linked to the neck or the back, fitting one who turned her back and returned to Moab.

expand to see more

Orpah — Hebrew Orpah, perhaps “neck” or “she who turns the back.”

She was a woman of Moab, the wife of Chilion.

She wept at the parting but turned back to her people.

She returned to her gods, the idols of Moab.

Her name and her parting alike speak of turning back.

Usage

"Like Orpah, many come near to faith with tears and good beginnings, yet draw back to the world."

"Orpah teaches that natural affection and warm feeling are not the same as saving faith."

"The woman who turned back warns that the LORD honours the one who cleaves to Him to the end."
